title: Transfer: Count Subarrays That Sum to K
oneLiner: Count the contiguous runs that add up to k, negatives allowed, in one pass: Two Sum's lookup, run on prefix sums.
keyTakeaway: A subarray sum is a difference of two prefix sums: sum(i..j) = prefix[j + 1] - prefix[i]. So "which earlier prefix makes this run equal k?" is "have I already seen prefix - k?", the same complement lookup as Two Sum, with a count per prefix instead of an index.
explanation:
This follows Two Sum, and it uses the prefix sums from Prefix Sums: Answer Range-Sum Queries. Given nums (negatives and zeros allowed) and k, return how many contiguous subarrays add up to exactly k. For [1, 2, 1, 2, 1] and k = 3 the answer is 4: [1, 2] twice and [2, 1] twice.

The brute force tries every start and every end, O(n^2). A sliding window does not rescue it: with negative numbers, growing the window can make the sum smaller, so you never know which end to move.

Write running for the sum of everything up to and including the current element, and say a run ending here starts just after some earlier point whose running sum was p. That run sums to running minus p. It equals k exactly when p = running - k. So at each element the question is: how many earlier prefixes had the value running - k? Keep a dictionary from prefix value to how many times it has occurred, seeded with {0: 1} for the empty prefix before the first element (that is what lets a run starting at index 0 count). For each number: add it to running, add counts[running - k] (0 if missing) to the answer, then record running in the map.

Order matters in the same way as in Two Sum: look up first, then record, so the current prefix never pairs with itself. One pass, O(n) time, O(n) space for the map.

The visualization runs [1, 2, 1, 2, 1] with k = 3; the tracker is the count so far.

Explain why the same idea works: before you move on, write two or three sentences comparing this with Two Sum. In Two Sum you looked up target - x among values you had already seen. What plays the role of x and of target here, why does the map store a count instead of an index, and why does the seed {0: 1} matter?

recognitionSignals: Count (or find) contiguous subarrays whose sum, or another additive total, equals a target.
Negative numbers are allowed, which rules out a sliding window.
gotchas: Seed the map with prefix 0 seen once, or every run that starts at index 0 is missed.
Look up running - k before you record running; recording first counts an empty run when k is 0.
Store how many times each prefix occurred, not just whether it occurred: [0, 0, 0] with k = 0 has six runs.
confusableWith: Sliding Window: Max Sum Subarray of Size K also looks at contiguous runs, but a window only works when every number is non-negative, so the sum grows as the window grows.

complexity.note: One pass with an O(1) average lookup and update per element; the map can hold a different prefix sum for every position.

referenceSolutions.python:
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    counts = {0: 1}  # the empty prefix
    running = 0
    found = 0
    for n in nums:
        running += n
        # Runs ending here that sum to k start after a prefix equal to running - k.
        found += counts.get(running - k, 0)
        counts[running] = counts.get(running, 0) + 1
    return found
